analysis.one_liner: Requires members of Congress and their families to put stocks and investments into blind trusts.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan bill to bar members of Congress from actively managing their own investments never got a hearing or a vote before the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: The TRUST in Congress Act would have required every member of Congress, along with their spouse and dependent children, to hand their individual stocks, commodities, and derivatives to an independent trustee in a qualified blind trust, so the lawmaker would not know what they own and could not trade on information learned in office [S2][S3]. Members could keep broad mutual funds and Treasury bonds. They would certify compliance to the Clerk of the House or Secretary of the Senate, and those certifications would be posted publicly [S3]. The bill was introduced by Rep. Abigail Spanberger, a Democrat, together with Rep. Chip Roy, a Republican, in June 2020 [S3], and never left committee.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, ordinary Americans would gain a Congress whose members cannot personally trade on legislation, hearings, or private briefings they receive. Members with potential conflicts would have to give up direct control of their investments until six months after leaving office.

how_it_helps.text: Members of Congress, their spouses, and dependent children must place covered investments — securities, commodities, futures, and derivatives — into a qualified blind trust within 90 days, and cannot dissolve or control them until 180 days after leaving office [S3].
Members must certify to the Clerk of the House or Secretary of the Senate that the trust exists or that they own no covered investments, and those certifications are posted on public websites [S3].
Blind trusts are an existing ethics tool: holdings are put under someone else's control specifically to avoid a possible conflict of interest [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Incumbent members of Congress and their families, who would lose the ability to buy and sell individual stocks, commodities, or derivatives while in office, and members with substantial portfolios who would bear the cost of trust administration.
analysis.who_pays_short: Members of Congress and their families

drawbacks.text: The bill relies on self-certification: a member certifies to the Clerk or Secretary that the trust is in place, and the exception clause allows a spouse or dependent child to keep a covered investment if it comes with their primary occupation [S3], which leaves room for assets to stay in the family's hands.

A member's own view, common among incumbents, is that existing financial disclosure laws already expose conflicts and that a forced blind trust adds administrative cost and could discourage some experienced people from serving. The bill also exempts widely held funds and Treasury securities, so members still hold diversified market exposure that can move with government policy [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public benefit — removing members' day-to-day control of trades in securities their own work can move — is real but hard to quantify, and the enforcement design is fairly light: certification plus public posting rather than audits or penalties [S3]. The main cost falls on lawmakers and their families, which is the point of the bill. Its main weakness is that it governs conduct that members themselves would certify, so skeptics can fairly ask whether compliance would have been meaningfully verified.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Committee on House Administration the day it was introduced and sat there without a hearing or a vote until the 116th Congress ended in January 2021, at which point it expired [S5][S1].

narrative.text: Rep. Abigail Spanberger (D-VA) introduced H.R. 7200 on June 15, 2020, together with Rep. Chip Roy (R-TX), and it was referred to the House Committee on House Administration the same day [S5][S3].
Eight members cosponsored the bill, split evenly: 4 of 231 House Democrats and 4 of 197 House Republicans [S4].
No further action was taken after the referral; the bill never received a committee vote, hearing listing, or floor vote before the Congress ended on January 3, 2021 [S5][S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Incumbent members of Congress are better off because the bill died: no one was required to give up direct control of their stock, commodity, or derivatives holdings while in office. Members who benefit from being able to trade individual securities avoided a binding change, and the issue was left for the next Congress to take up again.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was bipartisan from day one — a Democratic lead sponsor, a Republican original co-sponsor, and cosponsors split 4 Democrats and 4 Republicans — and it was stopped by committee inaction rather than by a partisan vote.

industries.industry: Members of Congress and their households
industries.note: The bill's only direct cost falls on sitting lawmakers and their spouses and dependent children, who would lose the ability to buy and sell individual securities, commodities, futures, and derivatives while in office. Lawmakers' interest in keeping that trading flexibility runs against the public interest in conflict-free lawmaking, which is why the bill sat without action in the committee that handles House ethics and administration matters [S3][S5].
